55	a surgical repair of the proximal adductor longus tendon
56	through a return-to-performance pathway. A case report
57	Andrew Mitchella and Craig Holdingb
58	a
59	Medical Department, RasenBallsport Leipzig GmbH, Leipzig, Germany; bIrish Football Association, Belfast,
60	Northern, Ireland
61	
62	
63	    ABSTRACT                                                                       ARTICLE HISTORY
64	    This case report details the management of a 23-year-old profes­               Received 24 June 2024
65	    sional footballer who sustained a rupture of the proximal adductor             Accepted 27 August 2024
66	    longus (AL) tendon. Following surgical reattachment of the tendon,             KEYWORDS
67	    the player completed an eleven-phase return to performance                     Criteria based; return to
68	    (RTPerf) pathway designed to ensure a rapid and safe return to play            performance pathway;
69	    (RTPlay). The pathway uses distinct phases that incorporate clinical,          professional football; surgical
70	    performance, and sport-specific criteria to guide decision-making              repair; adductor longus
71	    throughout the process. This case report outlines the phases and               tendon
72	    criteria used in conjunction with shared decision-making by the
73	    interdisciplinary team (IDT) to ensure a successful RTPlay. The effec­
74	    tiveness of this pathway was demonstrated by the player’s return to
75	    competitive play 12 weeks post-surgery.
76	
77	
78	
79	Introduction
80	Groin injuries are extremely common in football, accounting for 18% of all injuries (Mosler
81	et al., 2018). In addition, the AL muscle is reported to be involved in two-thirds (Mosler
82	et al., 2018) of all cases and 17% of these are classified as grade 3 injuries (rupture or
83	avulsion) (Serner et al., 2018). For grade 3 injuries, both conservative and surgical manage­
84	ment have provided solid RTPlay outcomes. Conservative management potentially pro­
85	vides shorter RTPlay times (10–12 weeks) (Dimitrakopoulou et al., 2008; Ueblacker et al.,
86	2016) and is better suited for small tendon retraction lengths (<2 cm), but carries the risk
87	of uncontrolled tendon healing, weakness and residual pain (Best et al., 2020). In contrast,
88	surgical management results in longer RTPlay times (12–16 weeks) (Best et al., 2020), but is
89	better suited to high-performance athletes that have suffered larger tendon retraction
90	lengths (>2 cm) and/or damage to other structures such as the pyramidalis muscle, the
91	anterior pubic ligament, and in some cases the pectineus muscle (Lempainen et al., 2021).
92	   The purpose of this case report is to describe how a professional footballer successfully
93	progressed through an RTPerf pathway following a proximal AL tendon reattachment. This
94	report will use the previously cited RTPerf pathway, which has 11 clear phases (Figure 1)
95	with clear progressions and objective criteria to help inform a shared decision-making
96	
97	
98	CONTACT Andrew Mitchell        andrew.mitchell@redbulls.com    Medical Department, RasenBallsport Leipzig GmbH,
99	Cottaweg 3, Leipzig 04177, Germany
100	© 2024 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group

112	movement jump; COD, change of direction; DECs, decelerations; Hams, hamstrings; LSG, large-sided games; M, metres; Max, maximum; MSG, medium-sided games;
113	Mins, minutes; Ms, milliseconds; NWB, non-weight bearing; RFD, rate of force development; SL, single leg; SSG, small-sided games; non-weight bearing; RFD, rate of
114	force development; SL, single leg; SSG, small-sided games.
115	                                                            RESEARCH IN SPORTS MEDICINE      3
116	
117	
118	process (Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024). The pathway has three distinct gym-based phases to
119	prepare the player for the subsequent grass phases. In conjunction with the grass phases,
120	the player will also complete more advanced gym profiling (power and reactive strength)
121	to ensure he is ready to resume team training (Grass Phase 4) and ultimately RTPlay (Grass
122	phase 5). The RTPerf pathway is completed (Grass Phase 6) when the player is deemed to
123	be performing at or above his previous level of performance.
124	
125	
126	
127	Discussion
128	Case presentation
129	This previously healthy 23-year-old professional footballer was playing centre-back in
130	a game when he attempted to clear a ball with his left foot. He immediately experienced
131	an audible “pop” and pain in the adductor region of the kicking limb. The injury mechan­
132	ism was established as abduction, extension and external rotation of the hip prior to
133	kicking the ball. This particular movement places a high eccentric load on the AL
134	(Charnock et al., 2009), with this particular mechanism accounting for 29% of all AL
135	ruptures (Serner et al., 2018). After attempting the clearance, the player was unable to
136	continue and was immediately removed from the field for clinical evaluation.
137	   From the outset, the player presented with common signs and symptoms of a proximal
138	AL tendon rupture. Initially, clinical assessment revealed a palpable defect/dip, swelling,
139	and reproduction of pain in the region of the adductor origin on outer range resistance
140	testing (Abate et al., 2023). Within 72 hours, the player underwent Magnetic resonance
141	imaging (MRI), which revealed a full-thickness avulsion of the AL origin and fibrocartilage
142	footprint. The tendon and fibrocartilage retracted distally 3.9 cm. Accompanying this
143	report, the player had developed an antalgic gait and gross swelling in the adductor
144	region. Compared to pre-injury metrics, he was significantly impaired in hip range of
145	movement (flexion, abduction and internal rotation), and strength output (resisted
146	adduction) at 0°, 45° and 90° of hip flexion. A shared decision-making process was
147	undertaken by key stakeholders (doctors, orthopaedic surgeon, physiotherapists, and
148	coaches), with the player (Dijkstra et al., 2017) electing for a proximal AL tendon reattach­
149	ment with a RTPlay goal of 12–16 weeks (Best et al., 2020).
150	
151	
152	
153	Surgical management and acute phase
154	Five days post-injury the player underwent surgery, where a 3–5 cm incision was made 3
155	cm distal to the pubic tubercle over the adductor region. The retracted AL tendon was
156	located and reattached to the pubic tubercle with 2 suture anchors. The subcutaneous
157	tissue was then closed with absorbable sutures and the skin was closed with non-
158	absorbable sutures (Lempainen et al., 2021). Immediately after surgery, appropriate
159	nutritional support, wound care, rest, and the use of cryotherapy were priorities. At 7
160	days postoperatively, the player was able to stop using crutches as he was able to adopt
161	a normal gait pattern and started a modified conditioning programme in the gym for the
162	upper body and the contralateral limb.
163	 4      A. MITCHELL AND C. HOLDING
164	
165	
166	Gym phase 1 - early loading and normal movement
167	During weeks 3–4 the player completed Gym Phase 1, regaining confidence in normal
168	movements such as squats and basic lunge patterns, first in the pool and then on land. In
169	the gym, regaining hip range of motion was prioritized along with the introduction of
170	adductor exercises using ball squeezes at 0°, 45° and 80–90° of hip flexion (Thorborg,
171	2023). These isometric exercises are believed to be beneficial for tendon loading and pain
172	reduction while promoting function (Hölmich et al., 1999). Prophylactic core stability
173	exercises were also introduced including basic plank positions, standing squat positions
174	and single leg (SL) balance-type exercises. Throughout this and subsequent phases, the
175	player used a numeric pain rating scale (0–10) to rate their pain, with 0 being no pain and
176	10 being the worst perceived pain. A score of 2 or less was considered acceptable for
177	exercise progression (Thorborg, 2023). Complementary to this, a global confidence rating
178	was used by the player to guide progression and ensure ongoing communication
179	between the player and the IDT (0% being no confidence and 100% being complete
180	confidence, with 80% required for progression) (Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024).
181	
182	
183	Gym phase 2 – reconditioning pathways
184	Once the player had demonstrated the basic movement patterns of Gym Phase 1, they
185	began Gym Phase 2, which focused on reconditioning pathways (Figure 1). This phase
186	lasted two and a half weeks as the player progressed through the various reconditioning
187	pathways in preparation for the return to running profiling in Gym Phase 3. Crucially,
188	adductor rehabilitation was a priority because of the surgical reattachment and its role in
189	football-related movements such as kicking and change of direction activities. Adductor
190	exercises included concentric and eccentric banded adduction, abduction, hip flexion,
191	and an introduction of multiplane combinations (Serner et al., 2020). Similarly, short lever
192	Copenhagen and standing slide board exercises were performed as pain and confidence
193	allowed (Serner et al., 2014). These, and the player’s overall reconditioning, were sup­
194	ported by exposure to the other pathways of this phase (Figure 1).
195	   The running preparation pathway included exercises such as wall drives, marching
196	patterns and low-level sled pushes. Player engagement and confidence was enhanced by
197	the indoor ball skills pathway, which used a stepwise approach to grading ball exercises
198	from seated foot contacts to 1-2 m passes, in this case. The plyometric pathway developed
199	the players’ ability to absorb and produce force through the stretch-shortening cycle
200	(SSC). This started in the pool with first double leg, and then SL exercises (squat jumps, to
201	countermovement to drop jump techniques), and progressed on a soft surface and,
202	towards the end of the phase, the normal gym floor (Mitchell et al., 2023).
203	   As with all the exercises in this phase, linear actions were performed first, followed by
204	the introduction of multidirectional patterns to gradually load the adductor region. The
205	injury specifics pathway inevitably included adductor progressions but also the develop­
206	ment of lumbo-pelvic control. Emphasis was placed on gluteal activation, avoidance of
207	anterior pelvic tilt and control of trunk stability to optimize load distribution through the
208	hip and groin region (King et al., 2018). Having progressed along the reconditioning
209	pathways of Gym Phase 2, the player was profiled in the return to running criteria (Gym
210	Phase 3) at weeks 6.5–7 to determine his readiness to run.

252	
253	Gym phase 3 – return to running `criteria checklist´
254	From the RTPerf pathway (Figure 1), Gym Phase 3 specifically profiles the player’s ability to
255	begin running and the introduction of sport-specific actions in Grass Phase 1. Minimum
256	standards surrounding the theme of return to running have been previously documented
257	(Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024) and were sufficiently met by this player during weeks 6.5–7. For
258	example, the player completed low-intensity running preparation sessions consisting of
259	A-skips, B-skips, butt kicks, and ankle bounds etc., in addition to an antigravity treadmill
260	session at 95% of the player’s body weight. The SSC was further evaluated by plyometric
261	profiling, which included a hop battery (profiled by distance achieved) and force plate
262	jumps (profiled by eccentric, concentric and performance variables such as jump height
263	and reactive strength index) (Mitchell et al., 2021, 2022). Player confidence, movement
264	proficiency and achieving 80% of pre-injury metrics were sufficient as 100% recovery of
265	 6      A. MITCHELL AND C. HOLDING
266	
267	
268	SSC qualities is not possible at this point in the process. Injury specific criteria such as
269	adductor squeeze and hip range of motion were all within 10% of pre-injury metrics
270	(Figure 2), which was further supported by players’ pain levels not exceeding 2/10. At 7
271	weeks post-surgery, an IDT decision based on the available date allowed the player to
272	progress to Grass Phase 1.
273	
274	
275	Grass phase 1 – reloading and technical reintroduction
276	At 7 weeks, the player began Grass Phase 1 (reloading and technical reintroduction),
277	which included the reintroduction of running, low-intensity sport-specific skills and the
278	completion of power profiling in the gym (Figure 1). Using live data monitoring (Global
279	Positioning System [GPS]), speeds were limited to <65% of a player’s maximum and
280	included a combination of pitch length runs (100 m), box-to-box runs (70 m) and football
281	specific dribbling circuits such as the Hoff Drill (Mitchell et al., 2023). Similarly, accelera­
282	tions (ACCs) and decelerations (DECs) were introduced (<65% of his maximal intensity)
283	but were confined to small spaces (≤4 m) to limit any exposure to high-speed running
284	(HSR) or high-intensity ACCs and DECs (Harper et al., 2022). In the gym, the player
285	continued to develop his power qualities and was profiled through the hop battery (SL
286	horizontal and triple hop techniques) and force plate (SL countermovement and drop)
287	jumps. Specific to this injury, underlying strength (adductor/abductor ratio and outer
288	range adductor strength, obtained from isometric profiling) (Mosler et al., 2017; Serner
289	et al., 2020), and dynamic power (SL medial and lateral hop techniques) were targeted in
290	conjunction with kicking actions using a resistance band. The normalization of these,
291	together with a meticulous progression of kicking loads (2 m to 10 m distances) on the
292	grass, improved player confidence, motivation and skill retraining.
293	
294	
295	Grass phase 2 – high speed running and agility drills
296	At 8 weeks, the player progressed to Grass Phase 2, which involved completing HSR and
297	intensive agility drills, including exercises with reactive decision-making. Running speeds
298	were increased to <85% of the player’s maximum speed, and the intensity of ACCs and
299	DECs was further increased by expanding the drill distances (Figure 1) (Harper et al., 2022).
300	The kicking distance was systematically increased from 10 m to 40 m while closely mon­
301	itoring the clinical signs, symptoms, and players’ ratings of self-confidence. In the gym,
302	reactive strength was profiled using the SL drop jump reactive strength index. Additionally,
303	the adductor strength was specifically targeted for recovery from this injury. The minimum
304	standards that needed to be met before entering Grass Phase 3 were an inner range
305	adductor/abductor strength ratio of 1.2 (±0.2) N (Mosler et al., 2017), and an outer range
306	isometric adductor strength >3.0 (±0.7) N·m/kg (Serner et al., 2020) in addition to other
307	sports-specific grass and gym-based metrics (Table 1) (Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024).
308	
309	
310	Grass phase 3 – maximum speed and positional drills
311	From weeks 9–10, the player completed the maximum speed and positional drills of Grass
312	Phase 3. Drills were often enhanced by the support of a technical coach or additional players
313	to replicate exercises that were chaotic and highly variable by design. Defending drills

331	involved long passing, clearing actions and blocking movements to enhance player con­
332	fidence in the injury. This was matched physically by the player achieving 94% of peak speed,
333	96% of peak ACC intensity, and 84% of peak DEC intensity (Table 1). In the gym, he continued
334	to work on hip and pelvic strength exercises (King et al., 2018) and adductor-specific exercises
335	(Serner et al., 2020), (Table 1) seeking further improvements and for prophylaxis. At the end of
336	Grass Phase 3, in addition to physical characteristics, the player expressed a confidence level
337	of over 90% in resuming team training (Grass Phase 4) in week 10.
338	
339	
340	Comparative outcomes
341	At 10 weeks, the IDT decision permitted the player to return to team training (Grass
342	Phase 4) and was reintroduced to passing drills, phases of play and small (4 vs 4),
343	medium (5 vs 5 to 8 vs 8) and large practice games (9 vs 9 to 11 vs 11). The player
344	was also exposed to peak running speeds (97%) and peak ACCs and DECs inten­
345	sities (98% and 99%, respectively) in training situations, helping him to replicate
346	match demands. Subsequently, at 12 weeks, he completed 45 min in a U23 match
347	without any complications (Grass Phase 5). Further match exposure was increased
348	over the next 2 weeks, allowing the player to participate fully in the regular match
349	schedule from 14 weeks (Grass Phase 6). Complementing these grass progressions
350	was the continuity of gym-based strength, power and reactive strength exercises,
351	helping to mitigate the risk of future injury (Lauersen et al., 2014).
352	
353	
354	Conclusion/Clinical implication
355	This case report demonstrates a successful RTPerf for a professional footballer who
356	sustained a rupture of the proximal AL tendon. Following an acute injury, the player
357	was effectively managed through surgical reattachment and adherence to a progressive
358	rehabilitation pathway. During the process, the player followed the RTPerf pathway, which
359	required him to meet phase-based clinical, psychological, and sports-specific criteria. The
360	RTPerf pathway was underpinned by the IDT’s shared decision-making, which aimed to
361	ensure a positive outcome and successful RTPerf.

a

Northern, Ireland


    ABSTRACT                                                                       ARTICLE HISTORY
    This case report details the management of a 23-year-old profes­               Received 24 June 2024
    sional footballer who sustained a rupture of the proximal adductor             Accepted 27 August 2024
    longus (AL) tendon. Following surgical reattachment of the tendon,             KEYWORDS
    the player completed an eleven-phase return to performance                     Criteria based; return to
    (RTPerf) pathway designed to ensure a rapid and safe return to play            performance pathway;
    (RTPlay). The pathway uses distinct phases that incorporate clinical,          professional football; surgical
    performance, and sport-specific criteria to guide decision-making              repair; adductor longus
    throughout the process. This case report outlines the phases and               tendon
    criteria used in conjunction with shared decision-making by the
    interdisciplinary team (IDT) to ensure a successful RTPlay. The effec­
    tiveness of this pathway was demonstrated by the player’s return to
    competitive play 12 weeks post-surgery.



Introduction
Groin injuries are extremely common in football, accounting for 18% of all injuries (Mosler
et al., 2018). In addition, the AL muscle is reported to be involved in two-thirds (Mosler
et al., 2018) of all cases and 17% of these are classified as grade 3 injuries (rupture or
avulsion) (Serner et al., 2018). For grade 3 injuries, both conservative and surgical manage­
ment have provided solid RTPlay outcomes. Conservative management potentially pro­
vides shorter RTPlay times (10–12 weeks) (Dimitrakopoulou et al., 2008; Ueblacker et al.,
2016) and is better suited for small tendon retraction lengths (<2 cm), but carries the risk
of uncontrolled tendon healing, weakness and residual pain (Best et al., 2020). In contrast,
surgical management results in longer RTPlay times (12–16 weeks) (Best et al., 2020), but is
better suited to high-performance athletes that have suffered larger tendon retraction
lengths (>2 cm) and/or damage to other structures such as the pyramidalis muscle, the
anterior pubic ligament, and in some cases the pectineus muscle (Lempainen et al., 2021).
   The purpose of this case report is to describe how a professional footballer successfully
progressed through an RTPerf pathway following a proximal AL tendon reattachment. This
report will use the previously cited RTPerf pathway, which has 11 clear phases (Figure 1)
with clear progressions and objective criteria to help inform a shared decision-making

movement jump; COD, change of direction; DECs, decelerations; Hams, hamstrings; LSG, large-sided games; M, metres; Max, maximum; MSG, medium-sided games;
Mins, minutes; Ms, milliseconds; NWB, non-weight bearing; RFD, rate of force development; SL, single leg; SSG, small-sided games; non-weight bearing; RFD, rate of
force development; SL, single leg; SSG, small-sided games.
                                                            RESEARCH IN SPORTS MEDICINE      3


process (Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024). The pathway has three distinct gym-based phases to
prepare the player for the subsequent grass phases. In conjunction with the grass phases,
the player will also complete more advanced gym profiling (power and reactive strength)
to ensure he is ready to resume team training (Grass Phase 4) and ultimately RTPlay (Grass
phase 5). The RTPerf pathway is completed (Grass Phase 6) when the player is deemed to
be performing at or above his previous level of performance.



Discussion
Case presentation
This previously healthy 23-year-old professional footballer was playing centre-back in
a game when he attempted to clear a ball with his left foot. He immediately experienced
an audible “pop” and pain in the adductor region of the kicking limb. The injury mechan­
ism was established as abduction, extension and external rotation of the hip prior to
kicking the ball. This particular movement places a high eccentric load on the AL
(Charnock et al., 2009), with this particular mechanism accounting for 29% of all AL
ruptures (Serner et al., 2018). After attempting the clearance, the player was unable to
continue and was immediately removed from the field for clinical evaluation.
   From the outset, the player presented with common signs and symptoms of a proximal
AL tendon rupture. Initially, clinical assessment revealed a palpable defect/dip, swelling,
and reproduction of pain in the region of the adductor origin on outer range resistance
testing (Abate et al., 2023). Within 72 hours, the player underwent Magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), which revealed a full-thickness avulsion of the AL origin and fibrocartilage
footprint. The tendon and fibrocartilage retracted distally 3.9 cm. Accompanying this
report, the player had developed an antalgic gait and gross swelling in the adductor
region. Compared to pre-injury metrics, he was significantly impaired in hip range of
movement (flexion, abduction and internal rotation), and strength output (resisted
adduction) at 0°, 45° and 90° of hip flexion. A shared decision-making process was
undertaken by key stakeholders (doctors, orthopaedic surgeon, physiotherapists, and
coaches), with the player (Dijkstra et al., 2017) electing for a proximal AL tendon reattach­
ment with a RTPlay goal of 12–16 weeks (Best et al., 2020).



Surgical management and acute phase
Five days post-injury the player underwent surgery, where a 3–5 cm incision was made 3
cm distal to the pubic tubercle over the adductor region. The retracted AL tendon was
located and reattached to the pubic tubercle with 2 suture anchors. The subcutaneous
tissue was then closed with absorbable sutures and the skin was closed with non-
absorbable sutures (Lempainen et al., 2021). Immediately after surgery, appropriate
nutritional support, wound care, rest, and the use of cryotherapy were priorities. At 7
days postoperatively, the player was able to stop using crutches as he was able to adopt
a normal gait pattern and started a modified conditioning programme in the gym for the
upper body and the contralateral limb.
 4      A. MITCHELL AND C. HOLDING


Gym phase 1 - early loading and normal movement
During weeks 3–4 the player completed Gym Phase 1, regaining confidence in normal
movements such as squats and basic lunge patterns, first in the pool and then on land. In
the gym, regaining hip range of motion was prioritized along with the introduction of
adductor exercises using ball squeezes at 0°, 45° and 80–90° of hip flexion (Thorborg,
2023). These isometric exercises are believed to be beneficial for tendon loading and pain
reduction while promoting function (Hölmich et al., 1999). Prophylactic core stability
exercises were also introduced including basic plank positions, standing squat positions
and single leg (SL) balance-type exercises. Throughout this and subsequent phases, the
player used a numeric pain rating scale (0–10) to rate their pain, with 0 being no pain and
10 being the worst perceived pain. A score of 2 or less was considered acceptable for
exercise progression (Thorborg, 2023). Complementary to this, a global confidence rating
was used by the player to guide progression and ensure ongoing communication
between the player and the IDT (0% being no confidence and 100% being complete
confidence, with 80% required for progression) (Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024).


Gym phase 2 – reconditioning pathways
Once the player had demonstrated the basic movement patterns of Gym Phase 1, they
began Gym Phase 2, which focused on reconditioning pathways (Figure 1). This phase
lasted two and a half weeks as the player progressed through the various reconditioning
pathways in preparation for the return to running profiling in Gym Phase 3. Crucially,
adductor rehabilitation was a priority because of the surgical reattachment and its role in
football-related movements such as kicking and change of direction activities. Adductor
exercises included concentric and eccentric banded adduction, abduction, hip flexion,
and an introduction of multiplane combinations (Serner et al., 2020). Similarly, short lever
Copenhagen and standing slide board exercises were performed as pain and confidence
allowed (Serner et al., 2014). These, and the player’s overall reconditioning, were sup­
ported by exposure to the other pathways of this phase (Figure 1).
   The running preparation pathway included exercises such as wall drives, marching
patterns and low-level sled pushes. Player engagement and confidence was enhanced by
the indoor ball skills pathway, which used a stepwise approach to grading ball exercises
from seated foot contacts to 1-2 m passes, in this case. The plyometric pathway developed
the players’ ability to absorb and produce force through the stretch-shortening cycle
(SSC). This started in the pool with first double leg, and then SL exercises (squat jumps, to
countermovement to drop jump techniques), and progressed on a soft surface and,
towards the end of the phase, the normal gym floor (Mitchell et al., 2023).
   As with all the exercises in this phase, linear actions were performed first, followed by
the introduction of multidirectional patterns to gradually load the adductor region. The
injury specifics pathway inevitably included adductor progressions but also the develop­
ment of lumbo-pelvic control. Emphasis was placed on gluteal activation, avoidance of
anterior pelvic tilt and control of trunk stability to optimize load distribution through the
hip and groin region (King et al., 2018). Having progressed along the reconditioning
pathways of Gym Phase 2, the player was profiled in the return to running criteria (Gym
Phase 3) at weeks 6.5–7 to determine his readiness to run.

Gym phase 3 – return to running `criteria checklist´
From the RTPerf pathway (Figure 1), Gym Phase 3 specifically profiles the player’s ability to
begin running and the introduction of sport-specific actions in Grass Phase 1. Minimum
standards surrounding the theme of return to running have been previously documented
(Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024) and were sufficiently met by this player during weeks 6.5–7. For
example, the player completed low-intensity running preparation sessions consisting of
A-skips, B-skips, butt kicks, and ankle bounds etc., in addition to an antigravity treadmill
session at 95% of the player’s body weight. The SSC was further evaluated by plyometric
profiling, which included a hop battery (profiled by distance achieved) and force plate
jumps (profiled by eccentric, concentric and performance variables such as jump height
and reactive strength index) (Mitchell et al., 2021, 2022). Player confidence, movement
proficiency and achieving 80% of pre-injury metrics were sufficient as 100% recovery of
 6      A. MITCHELL AND C. HOLDING


SSC qualities is not possible at this point in the process. Injury specific criteria such as
adductor squeeze and hip range of motion were all within 10% of pre-injury metrics
(Figure 2), which was further supported by players’ pain levels not exceeding 2/10. At 7
weeks post-surgery, an IDT decision based on the available date allowed the player to
progress to Grass Phase 1.


Grass phase 1 – reloading and technical reintroduction
At 7 weeks, the player began Grass Phase 1 (reloading and technical reintroduction),
which included the reintroduction of running, low-intensity sport-specific skills and the
completion of power profiling in the gym (Figure 1). Using live data monitoring (Global
Positioning System [GPS]), speeds were limited to <65% of a player’s maximum and
included a combination of pitch length runs (100 m), box-to-box runs (70 m) and football
specific dribbling circuits such as the Hoff Drill (Mitchell et al., 2023). Similarly, accelera­
tions (ACCs) and decelerations (DECs) were introduced (<65% of his maximal intensity)
but were confined to small spaces (≤4 m) to limit any exposure to high-speed running
(HSR) or high-intensity ACCs and DECs (Harper et al., 2022). In the gym, the player
continued to develop his power qualities and was profiled through the hop battery (SL
horizontal and triple hop techniques) and force plate (SL countermovement and drop)
jumps. Specific to this injury, underlying strength (adductor/abductor ratio and outer
range adductor strength, obtained from isometric profiling) (Mosler et al., 2017; Serner
et al., 2020), and dynamic power (SL medial and lateral hop techniques) were targeted in
conjunction with kicking actions using a resistance band. The normalization of these,
together with a meticulous progression of kicking loads (2 m to 10 m distances) on the
grass, improved player confidence, motivation and skill retraining.


Grass phase 2 – high speed running and agility drills
At 8 weeks, the player progressed to Grass Phase 2, which involved completing HSR and
intensive agility drills, including exercises with reactive decision-making. Running speeds
were increased to <85% of the player’s maximum speed, and the intensity of ACCs and
DECs was further increased by expanding the drill distances (Figure 1) (Harper et al., 2022).
The kicking distance was systematically increased from 10 m to 40 m while closely mon­
itoring the clinical signs, symptoms, and players’ ratings of self-confidence. In the gym,
reactive strength was profiled using the SL drop jump reactive strength index. Additionally,
the adductor strength was specifically targeted for recovery from this injury. The minimum
standards that needed to be met before entering Grass Phase 3 were an inner range
adductor/abductor strength ratio of 1.2 (±0.2) N (Mosler et al., 2017), and an outer range
isometric adductor strength >3.0 (±0.7) N·m/kg (Serner et al., 2020) in addition to other
sports-specific grass and gym-based metrics (Table 1) (Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024).


Grass phase 3 – maximum speed and positional drills
From weeks 9–10, the player completed the maximum speed and positional drills of Grass
Phase 3. Drills were often enhanced by the support of a technical coach or additional players
to replicate exercises that were chaotic and highly variable by design. Defending drills

involved long passing, clearing actions and blocking movements to enhance player con­
fidence in the injury. This was matched physically by the player achieving 94% of peak speed,
96% of peak ACC intensity, and 84% of peak DEC intensity (Table 1). In the gym, he continued
to work on hip and pelvic strength exercises (King et al., 2018) and adductor-specific exercises
(Serner et al., 2020), (Table 1) seeking further improvements and for prophylaxis. At the end of
Grass Phase 3, in addition to physical characteristics, the player expressed a confidence level
of over 90% in resuming team training (Grass Phase 4) in week 10.


Comparative outcomes
At 10 weeks, the IDT decision permitted the player to return to team training (Grass
Phase 4) and was reintroduced to passing drills, phases of play and small (4 vs 4),
medium (5 vs 5 to 8 vs 8) and large practice games (9 vs 9 to 11 vs 11). The player
was also exposed to peak running speeds (97%) and peak ACCs and DECs inten­
sities (98% and 99%, respectively) in training situations, helping him to replicate
match demands. Subsequently, at 12 weeks, he completed 45 min in a U23 match
without any complications (Grass Phase 5). Further match exposure was increased
over the next 2 weeks, allowing the player to participate fully in the regular match
schedule from 14 weeks (Grass Phase 6). Complementing these grass progressions
was the continuity of gym-based strength, power and reactive strength exercises,
helping to mitigate the risk of future injury (Lauersen et al., 2014).


Conclusion/Clinical implication
This case report demonstrates a successful RTPerf for a professional footballer who
sustained a rupture of the proximal AL tendon. Following an acute injury, the player
was effectively managed through surgical reattachment and adherence to a progressive
rehabilitation pathway. During the process, the player followed the RTPerf pathway, which
required him to meet phase-based clinical, psychological, and sports-specific criteria. The
RTPerf pathway was underpinned by the IDT’s shared decision-making, which aimed to
ensure a positive outcome and successful RTPerf.

No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).

Patient Signed Consent.



Author contributions
All authors take full responsibility for the writing, drafting and revisions of the manuscript. No other
external contributors are involved.

28	 "evidenceSummary": "Video analysis of male rugby union matches from England, New Zealand, South Africa, Portugal and the USA, across seven groups from U12 to Senior Elite, using a multilevel logistic regression of tackle success on tackle type and first point of contact. Active shoulder and smother tackles had the highest probability of success and arm tackles the lowest; in the junior groups, shoulder contact had a higher probability of success than mid-torso contact, while at senior levels the gap was small (for example, active shoulder tackles at Senior Elite: shoulder 86%, mid-torso 82%).",
29	 "screeningLimitations": "Video-coded tackle outcomes only, with no injury data, so the findings cannot show whether a contact height is safer. Only tackle type, contact point and a set of situational covariates were modelled, and tackle success was dichotomised, so the findings describe performance associations in male players only.",
30	 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the shoulder-contact advantage as a reason to coach shoulder contact at all levels, when the authors recommend mid-torso contact for safety and the performance gap at senior levels is only a few percentage points.",

32	  "year": 2025,

34	  "doi": "10.1002/ejsc.70003",
35	  "abstract": "The authors compared the probability of tackle success when the tackler first contacted the ball-carrier at the shoulder, mid-torso or legs, for active, passive, smother and arm tackles, across seven male playing groups. Video of 271 matches was analysed with multilevel logistic regression that adjusted for tackle direction, sequence, number of tacklers and attacking intention. Active shoulder tackles had the highest success probability across levels, and arm tackles the lowest.",
36	  "tldr": "Active shoulder and smother tackles were the most successful tackle types at every level from U16 upward, and arm tackles were the least successful. Shoulder contact beat mid-torso contact in the junior groups, but the senior difference was only a few percentage points.",
37	  "methods": "Cross-sectional video analysis of competitive male rugby matches coded with a consensus video framework. Tackle success was modelled with multilevel logistic regression (random effects for country and match), with tackle type and first contact point as the main terms and situational covariates held at observed values. Separate models were fitted for each playing group, and adjusted probabilities were reported with 95% CIs.",
38	  "findings": "At Senior Elite, the adjusted success probability for active shoulder tackles was 86% at the shoulder, 82% at mid-torso and 78% at the legs; arm tackles were 75%, 69% and 65%. Active shoulder and smother tackles did not differ significantly from each other from U16 upward. Junior groups (U12 to U18) generally showed higher success for shoulder contact than mid-torso contact, while at U12 leg contact was higher than mid-torso.",
39	  "limitations": "The abstract and text describe no difference between shoulder and mid-torso contact at senior levels, but Table 3 reports significant differences of about 4 percentage points at Senior Elite and Senior Amateur (p less than 0.001 for most tackle types); this report follows the table values. The title gives 52,204 tackles, the abstract and methods give 51,106, and the stated 271 matches does not match the group counts, which sum to 266. Only male players were studied, ball-carrier body position was not coded, and tackle success was dichotomised.",
40	  "practicalImplications": "Coaches can use the tackle-type ranking in training, with smother tackles treated as equal in importance to active shoulder tackles from U16. 41	  "athleteDev": "Success rates differ by age group, so tackle training can target the contact point and tackle type that are most successful for each age group. 40	    ABSTRACT
41	    To compare the probability of tackle success (the tackler preventing the ball‐carrier and ball from progressing towards the
42	    tackler try‐line) when contacting the ball‐carrier at different heights (shoulder, mid‐torso and legs) for different types of tackles
43	    (active, passive, smother and arm) while accounting for other tackler situational factors within seven playing levels. Video
44	    footage of 271 male rugby union matches were analysed across seven playing groups (Under [U] 12, n = 25 matches; U14,
45	    n = 35; U16, n = 39; U18 Amateur n = 39; U18 Elite n = 38; Senior Amateur, n = 40 and Senior Elite, n = 50) across England,
46	    New Zealand, South Africa, Portugal and USA (a total of 51,106 tackles). A multi‐level logistic regression model with tackle
47	    success as the outcome variable and first point of contact and type of tackle as the explanatory variables were computed.
48	    Included in the model as cofounders were the situational variables tackle direction, tackle sequence, number of players in the
49	    tackle and attacker intention. Post‐estimation marginal effects were used to calculate the probabilities (expressed as a per-
50	    centage %) of tackle success for each interaction between tackle type (active shoulder, smother, passive shoulder and arm) and
51	    the first point of contact (shoulder, mid‐torso and legs). The probability of tackle success in relation to where the ball‐carrier is
52	    contacted varied by tackle type and within each age group. The probabilities (Pr) for contacting the shoulder versus mid‐torso at
53	    the senior levels (elite and amateur) did not differ in relation to tackle success (for instance, for active shoulder tackles within
54	    senior elite; shoulder Pr 86% 95% CI 82–89 and mid‐torso Pr 82% 95% CI 77–86), whereas at the junior levels, contacting the
55	    shoulder had a higher probability than other points of contact. Active shoulder tackles had the highest probability of tackle
56	    success across the different playing levels across the different contact heights, whereas arm tackles had the lowest probability
57	    (for instance, for mid‐torso tackles within senior elite, active Pr 82% 95% CI 77–86 vs. arm Pr 69% 95% CI 64–75). Coaches and

    ABSTRACT
    To compare the probability of tackle success (the tackler preventing the ball‐carrier and ball from progressing towards the
    tackler try‐line) when contacting the ball‐carrier at different heights (shoulder, mid‐torso and legs) for different types of tackles
    (active, passive, smother and arm) while accounting for other tackler situational factors within seven playing levels. Video
    footage of 271 male rugby union matches were analysed across seven playing groups (Under [U] 12, n = 25 matches; U14,
    n = 35; U16, n = 39; U18 Amateur n = 39; U18 Elite n = 38; Senior Amateur, n = 40 and Senior Elite, n = 50) across England,
    New Zealand, South Africa, Portugal and USA (a total of 51,106 tackles). A multi‐level logistic regression model with tackle
    success as the outcome variable and first point of contact and type of tackle as the explanatory variables were computed.
    Included in the model as cofounders were the situational variables tackle direction, tackle sequence, number of players in the
    tackle and attacker intention. Post‐estimation marginal effects were used to calculate the probabilities (expressed as a per-
    centage %) of tackle success for each interaction between tackle type (active shoulder, smother, passive shoulder and arm) and
    the first point of contact (shoulder, mid‐torso and legs). The probability of tackle success in relation to where the ball‐carrier is
    contacted varied by tackle type and within each age group. The probabilities (Pr) for contacting the shoulder versus mid‐torso at
    the senior levels (elite and amateur) did not differ in relation to tackle success (for instance, for active shoulder tackles within
    senior elite; shoulder Pr 86% 95% CI 82–89 and mid‐torso Pr 82% 95% CI 77–86), whereas at the junior levels, contacting the
    shoulder had a higher probability than other points of contact. Active shoulder tackles had the highest probability of tackle
    success across the different playing levels across the different contact heights, whereas arm tackles had the lowest probability
    (for instance, for mid‐torso tackles within senior elite, active Pr 82% 95% CI 77–86 vs. arm Pr 69% 95% CI 64–75). Coaches and

15	Martin A. Lang1, Ross Tucker2, Suzi Edwards3, Grant L. Iverson4,5,6 and Andrew J. Gardner3*
16	
17	
18	  Abstract
19	  Background The rugby league tackle has been identified as the game event with the greatest propensity for a
20	  clinically diagnosed concussion. This study aims to replicate the work conducted in professional rugby league and
21	  rugby union by examining Head Injury Assessment (HIA) events to determine the associated tackle characteristics
22	  that increase concussion risk in sub-elite rugby league players. This comparison between competition levels is
23	  important due to the less developed physiological and tackle proficiency characteristics of sub-elite rugby league
24	  players and the fewer resources available for an on-field diagnosis, compared to the elite level of the sport.
25	  Results Tackles resulting in Head Injury Assessments (HIAs, n = 131) and 2,088 tackles that did not result in a head
26	  injury were identified and coded from one season of the 2019 Queensland Cup. The body position of both ball carrier
27	  and tackler, tackle height, and body contact areas were evaluated. The propensity for tacklers to undergo a head
28	  injury assessment was 1.49 HIAs per 1,000 tackles, equating to a 2.5-fold higher risk than that of the ball carrier (0.59
29	  HIAs per 1,000 tackles). The risk for an HIA was 2.75-fold greater when the tackler was upright (2.89 HIAs per 1,000
30	  tackles) compared to a bent-at-the-waist tackler (1.05 HIAs per 1,000 tackles). The greatest risk for the tackler and ball
31	  carrier sustaining an HIA occurred when the tackle height was high, with head-to-head contact having the greatest
32	  propensity for an HIA (44.37 HIAs per 1,000 tackles). HIA risk was also greater for both players when the ball carrier did
33	  not employ an evasion strategy (3.73 HIAs per 1,000 tackles).
34	  Conclusions The study replicates results from research in elite rugby league and rugby union. A combination of
35	  higher head contact/proximity and upright body position significantly increase an HIA risk. Tackler head position and
36	  ball carrier evasion behaviours also affect risk, suggesting that injury prevention strategies designed to reduce tackle
37	  height and improve tackle technique by focusing on head position, body position, and in a novel finding, ball carrier
38	  evasion, may reduce head injury risk in sub-elite rugby league players.

Tackle Risk Factors for Head Injury
Assessments (HIAs) in Sub-Elite Rugby League
and Recommendations for Prevention: Head
Contacts from Upright Tackles Increase the
HIA Risk to Both Ball Carrier and Tackler
Martin A. Lang1, Ross Tucker2, Suzi Edwards3, Grant L. Iverson4,5,6 and Andrew J. Gardner3*


  Abstract
  Background The rugby league tackle has been identified as the game event with the greatest propensity for a
  clinically diagnosed concussion. This study aims to replicate the work conducted in professional rugby league and
  rugby union by examining Head Injury Assessment (HIA) events to determine the associated tackle characteristics
  that increase concussion risk in sub-elite rugby league players. This comparison between competition levels is
  important due to the less developed physiological and tackle proficiency characteristics of sub-elite rugby league
  players and the fewer resources available for an on-field diagnosis, compared to the elite level of the sport.
  Results Tackles resulting in Head Injury Assessments (HIAs, n = 131) and 2,088 tackles that did not result in a head
  injury were identified and coded from one season of the 2019 Queensland Cup. The body position of both ball carrier
  and tackler, tackle height, and body contact areas were evaluated. The propensity for tacklers to undergo a head
  injury assessment was 1.49 HIAs per 1,000 tackles, equating to a 2.5-fold higher risk than that of the ball carrier (0.59
  HIAs per 1,000 tackles). The risk for an HIA was 2.75-fold greater when the tackler was upright (2.89 HIAs per 1,000
  tackles) compared to a bent-at-the-waist tackler (1.05 HIAs per 1,000 tackles). The greatest risk for the tackler and ball
  carrier sustaining an HIA occurred when the tackle height was high, with head-to-head contact having the greatest
  propensity for an HIA (44.37 HIAs per 1,000 tackles). HIA risk was also greater for both players when the ball carrier did
  not employ an evasion strategy (3.73 HIAs per 1,000 tackles).
  Conclusions The study replicates results from research in elite rugby league and rugby union. A combination of
  higher head contact/proximity and upright body position significantly increase an HIA risk. Tackler head position and
  ball carrier evasion behaviours also affect risk, suggesting that injury prevention strategies designed to reduce tackle
  height and improve tackle technique by focusing on head position, body position, and in a novel finding, ball carrier
  evasion, may reduce head injury risk in sub-elite rugby league players.

35	  "doi": "10.1136/bmjsem-2025-002612",
36	  "abstract": "The authors identified tackle characteristics associated with concussion for tacklers and ball-carriers in five seasons of English Premiership rugby union, using a case-control design. Of 231 video-identified concussions, 178 occurred to tacklers and 53 to ball-carriers, and these were compared with 9,963 control tackles. Lower tackles reduced the odds of concussion to ball-carriers, while the odds for tacklers were more nuanced but relatively low when contact was made with the ball-carrier's torso.",
37	  "tldr": "In elite rugby union, contacting the ball-carrier's torso carried relatively low concussion odds for both players, while head or neck contact with the ball-carrier was linked to high odds. A random forest selected key variables, and generalised linear mixed models with player as a random effect estimated odds ratios with 90% CIs.",
39	  "findings": "For tacklers, every head-contact location raised odds versus no head contact; head-to-torso raised them about 6.5-fold (OR 6.5, 90% CI 4.0 to 10.7) and was among the lowest of the head-contact categories, and head-to-knee had the highest odds (OR 155.8, 90% CI 75.3 to 322.4). Head-to-hip occurred most often and had the highest number of concussions per 1,000 tackles (3.1). For ball-carriers, head-to-head contact had the highest odds (OR 104.3, 90% CI 56.7 to 192.0), and first contact to the head or neck had higher odds than torso contact (OR 27.2, 90% CI 15.2 to 48.7).   "doi": "10.1136/bmjsem-2025-002612",
  "abstract": "The authors identified tackle characteristics associated with concussion for tacklers and ball-carriers in five seasons of English Premiership rugby union, using a case-control design. Of 231 video-identified concussions, 178 occurred to tacklers and 53 to ball-carriers, and these were compared with 9,963 control tackles. Lower tackles reduced the odds of concussion to ball-carriers, while the odds for tacklers were more nuanced but relatively low when contact was made with the ball-carrier's torso.",
  "tldr": "In elite rugby union, contacting the ball-carrier's torso carried relatively low concussion odds for both players, while head or neck contact with the ball-carrier was linked to high odds. Lower tackle height appears to reduce concussion risk for ball-carriers, but the tackler results are more mixed.",
  "methods": "Case-control study of male professional players in The English Premiership (2016/2017 to 2020/2021). Concussion cases were video-coded from club-reported events, and each was compared with control tackles from the same fixtures (25 tackles before and after the event). A random forest selected key variables, and generalised linear mixed models with player as a random effect estimated odds ratios with 90% CIs.",
  "findings": "For tacklers, every head-contact location raised odds versus no head contact; head-to-torso raised them about 6.5-fold (OR 6.5, 90% CI 4.0 to 10.7) and was among the lowest of the head-contact categories, and head-to-knee had the highest odds (OR 155.8, 90% CI 75.3 to 322.4). Head-to-hip occurred most often and had the highest number of concussions per 1,000 tackles (3.1). For ball-carriers, head-to-head contact had the highest odds (OR 104.3, 90% CI 56.7 to 192.0), and first contact to the head or neck had higher odds than torso contact (OR 27.2, 90% CI 15.2 to 48.7). The authors report that the random forest models had AUROC values of 0.73 to 0.84.",
  "limitations": "Only 54% of reported concussions could be identified on video, and ball-carrier events were harder to identify, which may bias the tackler-versus-ball-carrier comparison.   "practicalImplications": "Coaches and policy makers can use the finding that torso contact carries lower concussion odds for both players, supporting tackle-height strategies that target the torso.   "athleteDev": "Tackle training can focus on initial contact with the ball-carrier's torso and on keeping the tackler's head away from the ball-carrier's hip, knee and a teammate's head. Torso as the ball carrier's primary loading area had the lowest risk.",
37	  "tldr": "Tacklers who used their helmet, led with it, or placed their head across the ball carrier's path had higher concussion odds in matched NFL tackles. 40	  "limitations": "The sample was small, with 51 cases and 96 controls, and several variables produced undefined or very wide odds ratios. The study was funded by the NFL, and the author list includes an NFL employee and authors with consulting ties to the NFL.",

43	  "rtp": "Not applicable. The study examines tackle technique and concussion occurrence in NFL games and does not assess recovery, return-to-play decisions or post-concussion management."

9	Background: Concussions remain a major concern in football. A qualitative video review can provide contextual evidence sup-

11	Purpose: To identify tackling techniques and characteristics associated with concussions to the tackling player.
12	Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
13	Methods: A qualitative review of 51 concussions sustained by tacklers in National Football League (NFL) games between the
14	2015 and 2019 seasons as well as 96 control tackles was performed using video from multiple perspectives. For each concussive
15	case, 1 to 3 nonconcussive control tackles were matched based on player trajectory and closing speed as determined from
16	on-field player tracking data from Next Gen Stats. Cases and controls were coded for 20 different tackle techniques and char-
17	acteristics. The data were analyzed using conditional logistic regression models, and the results were expressed as odds ratios
18	(ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) as well as adjusted and unadjusted P values.
19	Results: Despite attempting to match cases and controls based on closing velocity, closing velocity was significantly associated
20	with the concussion risk in every logistic regression model. Predictors that had the greatest effect on the increased risk of con-
21	cussions were ‘‘tackler leading with helmet’’ (OR, 5.18 [95% CI, 1.87-14.33]; false discovery rate [FDR]–adjusted P = .0032) and

Tackle Techniques and Characteristics
Associated With a Concussion in Tackling
Players in the National Football League
Christopher P. Sherwood,*y MS , Fintan Grogan,z BSc ,
Timothy L. McMurry,§ PhD , James R. Funk,y PhD, PE , Jeff R. Crandall,y PhD,
Allen Sills,|| MD , and Gregory Tierney,{ PhD
Investigation performed at Biomechanics Consulting and Research, Charlottesville, Virginia, USA

Background: Concussions remain a major concern in football. A qualitative video review can provide contextual evidence sup-
porting changes in rules and coaching techniques aimed at reducing the risk of players sustaining a concussion.
Purpose: To identify tackling techniques and characteristics associated with concussions to the tackling player.
Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
Methods: A qualitative review of 51 concussions sustained by tacklers in National Football League (NFL) games between the
2015 and 2019 seasons as well as 96 control tackles was performed using video from multiple perspectives. For each concussive
case, 1 to 3 nonconcussive control tackles were matched based on player trajectory and closing speed as determined from
on-field player tracking data from Next Gen Stats. Cases and controls were coded for 20 different tackle techniques and char-
acteristics. The data were analyzed using conditional logistic regression models, and the results were expressed as odds ratios
(ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) as well as adjusted and unadjusted P values.
Results: Despite attempting to match cases and controls based on closing velocity, closing velocity was significantly associated
with the concussion risk in every logistic regression model. Predictors that had the greatest effect on the increased risk of con-
cussions were ‘‘tackler leading with helmet’’ (OR, 5.18 [95% CI, 1.87-14.33]; false discovery rate [FDR]–adjusted P = .0032) and
‘‘tackler primary loading’’ being the helmet as opposed to the shoulder (OR, 4.61 [95% CI, 1.41-15.05]; FDR-adjusted P = .0000).
Important factors associated with a reduced concussion risk were the tackler’s ‘‘head placed on correct side’’ of the ball carrier
(OR, 4.17 [95% CI, 1.58-11.01]; FDR-adjusted P = .0088) and ‘‘ball carrier primary loading,’’ with the torso having the lowest risk
relative to all other body segments.
Conclusion: The less a tackler involved his helmet in a tackle, the lower his risk of sustaining a concussion. This study supports
teaching players to place their heads on the correct side of the ball carrier (neither into the ball carrier nor into the path of the ball
carrier) when tackling to reduce their risk of a concussion, and players should target the torso of the ball carrier as their primary
contact point.
Keywords: football; video review; concussion; injury prevention

11	 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
12	 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],

15	 "populations":["Male Athletes","Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
16	 "evidenceSummary":"Video analysis of 74 tackle-related moderate and severe injuries (at least 8 days lost; 31 tacklers, 43 ball-carriers) from the South African Currie Cup, 2014 to 2018, each compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free tackles. Injury-causing tackles scored lower on standardised technical checklists than both the same player's injury-free tackles and teammates' injury-free tackles; for example, injured front-on tacklers scored 6.19 of 16 versus 8.90 for own controls and 9.93 for team controls.",
17	 "screeningLimitations":"The analysis used a single analyst, a univariate comparison without adjustment for situational factors, and checklists validated mainly for shoulder and arm tackles. Only 74 of 288 moderate and severe contact injuries could be matched to video, so the injured sample is selected.",
18	 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the lower technique scores as proof that poor technique caused these injuries, when the study shows that injury-causing tackles were less technically proficient than matched uninjured tackles, not that the technique gap is the cause.",
19	 "paper":{
20	   "year":2021,
21	   "citation":"Meintjes V, Forshaw P, den Hollander S, et al. Tackler and ball-carrier technique during moderate and severe injuries (≥8 days lost) compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free controls in Elite Rugby Union. Br J Sports Med. 2021;0:1-10.",
22	   "doi":"10.1136/bjsports-2020-103759",
23	   "abstract":"The authors scored tackler and ball-carrier technique in 74 moderate and severe (8 or more days lost) tackle injuries in the Currie Cup from 2014 to 2018. Each injury was compared with injury-free tackles by the same player and by teammates. Overall technical proficiency was significantly lower for the injury-causing event than for both control groups, for tacklers and ball-carriers, in front-on and side-on or behind tackles.",
24	   "tldr":"Tacklers and ball-carriers who were injured in moderate or severe tackle injuries in the Currie Cup scored lower on technique checklists than their own uninjured tackles and their teammates' uninjured tackles. The study identifies specific technique gaps that coaches can target in training.",
25	   "methods":"Case-control study using video from South African Rugby Union injury surveillance. For each injury, matched injury-free tackles by the same player (own controls) and by teammates (team controls) were identified within the same or most recent match, matched on tackle type, direction and role, with a target ratio of 1:5:5. A single analyst scored technical criteria on a 16-point or 11-point scale for tacklers and 14-point or 12-point scale for ball-carriers, and groups were compared with one-way ANOVA, Tukey post hoc tests and effect sizes.",
26	   "findings":"For front-on tackles, injured tacklers scored 6.19 of 16 (95% CI 4.89 to 7.48), compared with 8.90 for own controls and 9.93 for team controls. For side-on or behind tackles, injured tacklers scored 4.80 of 11, compared with 6.44 and 7.23. For ball-carriers, injured players scored 5.60 of 14 (front-on) and 5.17 of 12 (side-on or behind), compared with 8.08 and 8.16, and 7.39 and 7.75, respectively. Front-on tacklers who were injured were repeatedly weaker at moving from upright to a bent-at-waist position and at making shoulder contact first.",
27	   "limitations":"The analysis was univariate and did not adjust for player physical attributes, playing position, match context or the opponent's actions, and the authors note that technique scoring includes subjectivity. Only shoulder and arm tackles in front-on and side-on or behind direction were analysed, and 74 of 288 moderate and severe contact injuries could be matched to video. The sample comes from one domestic competition over five seasons, so the results may not generalise to other competitions.",
28	   "practicalImplications":"Coaches and trainers can use the listed technique gaps to design tackle training, for example upright-to-bent body position and shoulder-first contact for tacklers, and shifting the ball and protecting it in the correct arm for ball-carriers. The authors suggest building team databases of technique scores to find individual deficits.",
29	   "athleteDev":"The study points to specific tackler techniques (keeping the back straight with the centre of gravity ahead, head on the correct side, head up and forward, using the arms after contact, and releasing the ball carrier) and ball-carrier techniques (awareness of the tackler, shifting the ball to the correct arm, explosiveness, and going to ground to present the ball) that scored lower in injury-causing tackles.",
30	   "rtp":"The authors suggest that knowing which techniques a player lacks could help the return-to-contact process and reduce re-injury risk, but the study did not test this. The technique scores therefore cannot be used as a return-to-play criterion on the basis of this paper."
31	 }

 "evidenceSummary":"Video analysis of 74 tackle-related moderate and severe injuries (at least 8 days lost; 31 tacklers, 43 ball-carriers) from the South African Currie Cup, 2014 to 2018, each compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free tackles. Injury-causing tackles scored lower on standardised technical checklists than both the same player's injury-free tackles and teammates' injury-free tackles; for example, injured front-on tacklers scored 6.19 of 16 versus 8.90 for own controls and 9.93 for team controls.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The analysis used a single analyst, a univariate comparison without adjustment for situational factors, and checklists validated mainly for shoulder and arm tackles. Only 74 of 288 moderate and severe contact injuries could be matched to video, so the injured sample is selected.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the lower technique scores as proof that poor technique caused these injuries, when the study shows that injury-causing tackles were less technically proficient than matched uninjured tackles, not that the technique gap is the cause.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Meintjes V, Forshaw P, den Hollander S, et al. Tackler and ball-carrier technique during moderate and severe injuries (≥8 days lost) compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free controls in Elite Rugby Union. Br J Sports Med. 2021;0:1-10.",
   "doi":"10.1136/bjsports-2020-103759",
   "abstract":"The authors scored tackler and ball-carrier technique in 74 moderate and severe (8 or more days lost) tackle injuries in the Currie Cup from 2014 to 2018. Each injury was compared with injury-free tackles by the same player and by teammates. Overall technical proficiency was significantly lower for the injury-causing event than for both control groups, for tacklers and ball-carriers, in front-on and side-on or behind tackles.",
   "tldr":"Tacklers and ball-carriers who were injured in moderate or severe tackle injuries in the Currie Cup scored lower on technique checklists than their own uninjured tackles and their teammates' uninjured tackles. The study identifies specific technique gaps that coaches can target in training.",
   "methods":"Case-control study using video from South African Rugby Union injury surveillance. For each injury, matched injury-free tackles by the same player (own controls) and by teammates (team controls) were identified within the same or most recent match, matched on tackle type, direction and role, with a target ratio of 1:5:5. A single analyst scored technical criteria on a 16-point or 11-point scale for tacklers and 14-point or 12-point scale for ball-carriers, and groups were compared with one-way ANOVA, Tukey post hoc tests and effect sizes.",
   "findings":"For front-on tackles, injured tacklers scored 6.19 of 16 (95% CI 4.89 to 7.48), compared with 8.90 for own controls and 9.93 for team controls. For side-on or behind tackles, injured tacklers scored 4.80 of 11, compared with 6.44 and 7.23. For ball-carriers, injured players scored 5.60 of 14 (front-on) and 5.17 of 12 (side-on or behind), compared with 8.08 and 8.16, and 7.39 and 7.75, respectively. Front-on tacklers who were injured were repeatedly weaker at moving from upright to a bent-at-waist position and at making shoulder contact first.",
   "limitations":"The analysis was univariate and did not adjust for player physical attributes, playing position, match context or the opponent's actions, and the authors note that technique scoring includes subjectivity. Only shoulder and arm tackles in front-on and side-on or behind direction were analysed, and 74 of 288 moderate and severe contact injuries could be matched to video. The sample comes from one domestic competition over five seasons, so the results may not generalise to other competitions.",
   "practicalImplications":"Coaches and trainers can use the listed technique gaps to design tackle training, for example upright-to-bent body position and shoulder-first contact for tacklers, and shifting the ball and protecting it in the correct arm for ball-carriers.    "athleteDev":"The study points to specific tackler techniques (keeping the back straight with the centre of gravity ahead, head on the correct side, head up and forward, using the arms after contact, and releasing the ball carrier) and ball-carrier techniques (awareness of the tackler, shifting the ball to the correct arm, explosiveness, and going to ground to present the ball) that scored lower in injury-causing tackles.",
   "rtp":"The authors suggest that knowing which techniques a player lacks could help the return-to-contact process and reduce re-injury risk, but the study did not test this. The technique scores therefore cannot be used as a return-to-play criterion on the basis of this paper."

20	   "year":2021,
21	   "citation":"Meintjes V, Forshaw P, den Hollander S, et al. Tackler and ball-carrier technique during moderate and severe injuries (≥8 days lost) compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free controls in Elite Rugby Union. Br J Sports Med. 2021;0:1-10.",
22	   "doi":"10.1136/bjsports-2020-103759",
23	   "abstract":"The authors scored tackler and ball-carrier technique in 74 moderate and severe (8 or more days lost) tackle injuries in the Currie Cup from 2014 to 2018. Each injury was compared with injury-free tackles by the same player and by teammates. Overall technical proficiency was significantly lower for the injury-causing event than for both control groups, for tacklers and ball-carriers, in front-on and side-on or behind tackles.",
24	   "tldr":"Tacklers and ball-carriers who were injured in moderate or severe tackle injuries in the Currie Cup scored lower on technique checklists than their own uninjured tackles and their teammates' uninjured tackles. The study identifies specific technique gaps that coaches can target in training.",
25	   "methods":"Case-control study using video from South African Rugby Union injury surveillance. For each injury, matched injury-free tackles by the same player (own controls) and by teammates (team controls) were identified within the same or most recent match, matched on tackle type, direction and role, with a target ratio of 1:5:5. A single analyst scored technical criteria on a 16-point or 11-point scale for tacklers and 14-point or 12-point scale for ball-carriers, and groups were compared with one-way ANOVA, Tukey post hoc tests and effect sizes.",
26	   "findings":"For front-on tackles, injured tacklers scored 6.19 of 16 (95% CI 4.89 to 7.48), compared with 8.90 for own controls and 9.93 for team controls. For side-on or behind tackles, injured tacklers scored 4.80 of 11, compared with 6.44 and 7.23. For ball-carriers, injured players scored 5.60 of 14 (front-on) and 5.17 of 12 (side-on or behind), compared with 8.08 and 8.16, and 7.39 and 7.75, respectively. Front-on tacklers who were injured were repeatedly weaker at moving from upright to a bent-at-waist position and at making shoulder contact first.",
27	   "limitations":"The analysis was univariate and did not adjust for player physical attributes, playing position, match context or the opponent's actions, and the authors note that technique scoring includes subjectivity. Only shoulder and arm tackles in front-on and side-on or behind direction were analysed, and 74 of 288 moderate and severe contact injuries could be matched to video. The sample comes from one domestic competition over five seasons, so the results may not generalise to other competitions.",
28	   "practicalImplications":"Coaches and trainers can use the listed technique gaps to design tackle training, for example upright-to-bent body position and shoulder-first contact for tacklers, and shifting the ball and protecting it in the correct arm for ball-carriers. The authors suggest building team databases of technique scores to find individual deficits.",
29	   "athleteDev":"The study points to specific tackler techniques (keeping the back straight with the centre of gravity ahead, head on the correct side, head up and forward, using the arms after contact, and releasing the ball carrier) and ball-carrier techniques (awareness of the tackler, shifting the ball to the correct arm, explosiveness, and going to ground to present the ball) that scored lower in injury-causing tackles.",
30	   "rtp":"The authors suggest that knowing which techniques a player lacks could help the return-to-contact process and reduce re-injury risk, but the study did not test this. The technique scores therefore cannot be used as a return-to-play criterion on the basis of this paper."
31	 }

Full-body 3D motion capture (300 Hz) was used, and mixed general linear models compared peak resultant linear and angular head accelerations across instructions.",

29	   "athleteDev":"The study supports coaching tacklers to keep the head up and forward, keep the back straight and put the head outside the ball carrier's shoulder. 30	   "rtp":"Not applicable. The study measures head kinematics in healthy players during slow simulated tackles and does not assess concussion, recovery or return-to-play decisions."
