90	uccessful front-on, one-on-one torso tackle trials completed by 15 rugby-code players using three-
91	dimensional motion capture were recorded. Tackles differed with respects to the height of the
92	contact point on the ball carrier’s torso. A series of mixed general linear models were conducted.
93	Results: The tackler sustained the highest peak resultant linear (p<0.001) and angular (p<0.01)
94	head accelerations when contacting the lower torso to execute a ‘dominant’ tackle compared to
95	mid or upper torso, although these latter tackle types had the lowest ball carrier inertial head
96	kinematics. When executing a ‘smother’ tackle technique, a significant decrease in peak resultant
97	linear head acceleration was observed with a vertical ‘pop’ then lock action employed, compared
98	to the traditional upper torso tackling technique (p<0.001). Conclusions: Modifying the tackler’s
99	engagement with a ball carrier’s torso, with respect to height and technical execution, alters the
100	inertial head kinematics of the tackler and the ball carrier. The traditional thinking about optimal
101	tackle technique, as instructed, may need to be re-evaluated with the mid-torso a potential
102	alternative target contact height, while changes in tackle execution may be relatively protective for
103	tacklers when executing either a ‘dominant’ or ‘smother’ tackle. This study provides critical
104	cientific evidence to underpin revised coaching tackling technique interventions that might
105	enhance player safety. Tackles in which the tackler contacts the ball carrier around the mid torso
106	region, rather than lower torso, produce the lowest acceleration, and thus may contribute to
107	reducing head injury risk for the tackler.
108	Key Words: MOTION CAPTURE; HEAD; CONCUSSION; BIOMECHANICS
109	 INTRODUCTION
110	        The rugby codes are popular international collision sports. There are 6.1 million rugby
111	union players globally, including 3.9 million in Europe, 1.8 million in Rugby North America, and
112	1.1 million in Oceania (1). Numerous physical collisions (2) occur in game play, in which the
113	defensive players (called the tacklers) attempt to prevent the attacking player (called the ball
114	carrier) from scoring. Most elite-level rugby league players perform an average of 11 to 30 tackles
115	per player per game (3), with some players performing up to 54 tackles per player per game (4).
116	Elite rugby union players typically perform between 4 and 14 successful tackles per game (5).
117	        The tackle event has the greatest risk for concussion (6-11). Approximately 15.4 [95% CI
118	9.5 to 21.3](12) to 20.4 (11) concussions occurred per 1,000 player match hours in professional
119	rugby union, and approximately 14.8 [95% CI 9.6 to 23.0](8) in professional rugby league (13).
120	Online coaching instruction of safer tackling techniques and for reducing concussion risk is offered
121	by many rugby code governing bodies [e.g., the National Rugby League (NRL) Tackle Safe (14)
122	(www.playrugbyleague.com/), RugbySmart (15) (www.rugbysmart.co.nz/), and BokSmart (16)
123	(www.boksmart.com)]. The evidence informing the content of these injury reduction programmes
124	to reduce concussion risk is limited (17). The programmes are also often based on expert opinion
125	rather than empirical evidence (16), and as a result, the tackling coaching content taught within
126	these programmes is informed largely by coaching insight and not scientific evidence. It remains
127	unknown whether or not the content underpinning these tackle interventions results in safer
128	tackling and promotes player safety. For example, the evidence underpinning the NRL Tackle Safe
129	(14) program is based on a small study with elite rugby union players (18) (not rugby league
130	players). The manual identifies a mid-level injury danger area (i.e., ‘orange zone’) when the tackler
131	 contacts the ball carrier at the mid torso (between the ball carrier’s top of pelvis and base of
132	chest/pectorals), but the safest area or ‘green zone’ is claimed to be when the tackler contacts the
133	ball carrier on the lower torso, the hip area. This colour zone system is not supported by recent
134	evidence in professional rugby league (19), where the lowest propensity for HIAs was when the
135	tackler contacts the ball carrier’s torso (i.e., mid-torso), and the highest propensity (excluding rare
136	events with a low incidence e.g. boot) and most frequent impact sites are when the tackler contacts
137	the torso either too high (i.e., upper torso, or above the sternum/chest) or low (i.e., hip area). This
138	uggests that the NRL Tackle Safe program (14) may incorrectly identify the safest contact area,
139	and that a reassessment of tackle education based on this colour zone system is warranted.
140	        Despite 95% of concussions in professional rugby league occurring during the tackle (20),
141	the mechanistic understanding of how tackling technique influences head impact is poorly
142	understood. During a tackle, impulsive forces (incurred through rapid acceleration and
143	deceleration) are applied either directly or indirectly to the head, transferring forces to the brain.
144	These forces can result in a concussion by placing strain on tether points within the brain that may
145	lead to axonal stress, neuroinflammation, and a neurometabolic cascade (21), that may display as
146	post-concussion symptoms. These impulsive forces repetitively sustained but that do not lead a
147	concussion diagnosis (i.e., sub-concussive impact) (22) including from tackling (23) are postulated
148	to be linked to neurological issues, though emerging evidence remain inclusive to date (22).
149	Whether the injury mechanism is a single event or culminative incidents, reducing the magnitude
150	of inertial head kinematics of a single tackle or across hundreds of tackles will both achieve an
151	effect to reduce the risk of concussion when tackling regardless of either mechanism.
152	         Accurate in-game three-dimensional (3D) tackling methodologies to measure 3D head
153	kinematics do not currently exist (24). In the laboratory, 3D retroreflective motion analysis is the
154	gold standard for measuring 3D movement. It provides an understanding of 3D head kinematics
155	during the tackle and provides an opportunity to examine the risks of head impact associated with
156	various tackle techniques. However, the 3D retroreflection motion analysis tackle technique
157	literature measured in the laboratory is emerging (24). The ball carrier has previously been found
158	to experience greater changes in head angular velocity and angular acceleration in one-on-one,
159	front-on, tackles in a upper torso, compared to a low (25) or mid/low torso (26) tackle height.
160	        The objective of this study was to investigate how four types of successfully executed,
161	legal front-on, one-on-one torso tackles influence the tackler’s and ball carrier’s inertial head
162	kinematics. It was hypothesised that the tackle techniques (i.e., the Dominant, Torso & Stick (DTS)
163	and the Smother Ball, Pop & Lock (SLP), described subsequently) that adhere most closely to
164	tackles with the lowest propensity for HIAs (i.e., mid-torso)(19, 27) would result in significantly
165	decreased peak head linear and angular acceleration for the tackler compared to hip area contact
166	(Dominant NRL, DNRL) or upper torso area (Smother NRL, SNRL).
167	METHODS
168	Participants
169	        Amateur or semi-professional healthy, uninjured, male, adult rugby league or rugby union
170	players (n = 15) were recruited from grade competitions. The player characteristics of interest
171	included: sport played (i.e., rugby league or rugby union), participant history in the sport(s) (i.e.,
172	playing experience in years played), and highest competition level played. At the time of data
173	 collection, each participant’s age, current competition level, and playing position(s) were recorded.
174	It was deemed a sample size of 14 participants was sufficient based on using previous published
175	data of the tacklers’ trunk flexion angle at contact when performing an upper and lower torso tackle
176	(28). The power calculation was determined for two-tailed t-tests with an error probability and
177	tatistical power of 95% using G*Power software (29). Each participant provided written,
178	informed consent prior to their participation. The University of Newcastle Human Research Ethics
179	Committee (H-2017-0285) approved the study design and methodology.
180	Experimental Procedures
181	        Each data collection session involved two participants, one initially allocated the ball
182	carrier role, and the other participant the tackler role. Participants provided informed consent,
183	completed a questionnaire of their sporting participation, and then their anthropometric
184	measurements were recorded for later input into a mathematical model (i.e., body mass, height,
185	and pelvis, xyphoid, and chest depths). Standing in the anatomical position, a static measurement
186	of both participants was recorded. The expert coach guided participants to perform a set of 10 trials
187	of one of four different one-on-one, front-on, torso tackle techniques (see Supplemental Digital
188	Content 1, Supplemental Figure 1, Schematic diagram of data collection of the 80 trials performed
189	within a session, http://links.lww.com/MSS/C569) (30). The NRL coaching manual (31) was
190	followed to guide the instruction of two tackling techniques where the tackler’s shoulder contacted
191	the upper torso (SNRL) or hip area (DNRL) of the ball carrier, respectively. The other two tackling
192	techniques were novel variations of the NRL tackles. They involved tacklers being instructed to
193	modify their actions during the contact with the ball carrier: (i) with the tackler lowering the
194	vertical height of his body position and then performing a vertical ‘pop up’ action that reorients
195	 the motion of the ball carrier into an upward direction (SLP); and (ii) by marginally increasing the
196	contact height from hip area to mid-torso and redirecting the ball carrier into a vertical and
197	backward direction (DTS).
198	        A set of either DNRL or SNRL tackles were always completed first, in a counterbalanced
199	order. Then participants performed a set of the modified tackle technique (DTS or SLP). Each set
200	consisted of five dominant shoulder engagements by the tackler, followed by five trials of non-
201	dominant shoulder side engagements. This was implemented in this study due to ambiguous
202	evidence as to whether dominant and non-dominant shoulder engagement alters tackle technique
203	(32, 33).
204	        The expert coach instructed the participants on how to perform the specific technique
205	correctly, prior to participants engaging in the 10 trials of that technique. Several familiarisation
206	trials of that technique were performed with coaching feedback delivered. The coach evaluated
207	every tackle repetition and deemed it successful if, in his assessment, the correct technique had
208	been executed. Reasons for rejection of a tackle attempt included if the tackler’s head was not on
209	the side of the ball carrier’s body (right shoulder side tackle, left side of ball carrier’s body) or the
210	ball carrier was holding the ball on the incorrect side (Figure 1).
211	A       After the participants completed the 40 tackle trials (4 types, 10 trials per type), the roles
212	of the participants were reversed (i.e., the tackler became the ball carrier and vice-versa), another
213	tatic trial in the anatomical position was performed, followed by another 40 (4 types, 10 of each)
214	tackling trials. The total experimental protocol lasted approximately three hours.
215	 Expert Coach
216	        The expert coach for this study was a recently retired dual international rugby league and
217	rugby union representative player, with junior and senior rugby league and rugby union coaching
218	experience. This expert coach developed the non-traditional front-on tackle technique (SLP, DTS)
219	employed in this study. All sessions were attended by the expert coach who gave coaching
220	instruction to all participants prior to them undertaking the data collection session. The coach also
221	provided guidance and feedback to all participants throughout each session.
222	Tackling Trials
223	        Every trial started with the ball carrier and tackler in a stationary position, ~4 metres apart.
224	To standardise the approach speed, thereby limiting the confounding factor of player speed (10,
225	34), the participants were instructed to simultaneously run towards each engaging in contact at
226	80% game intensity, while each player speed was measured using the three-dimensional motion
227	caption system. This instruction led to a slow tackle speed (as per the definition of walking or
228	jogging into the tackle).
229	  C     The tackle was not completed to the ground in this study: (i) because player contact, rather
230	than ground contact, causes most tackle injuries (35); as well as (ii) the injury risk for the
231	participants that is associated with the skin mounted retroreflective markers impacting with the
232	ground. As a result, tackles in this study were done at slower speed with less force (i.e., 80% game
233	intensity) than would typically occur in field situations in training and matches. The tackle surface
234	was a 20 m2 matted surface [1000 x 1000 x 40 mm jigsaw mat underlay, 2000 x 1000 x 40 mm
235	 Tatami Judo mat (Southern Cross Mats, Sydney, NSW & Melbourne, Victoria)]. Rest periods were
236	30 seconds between trials, and ~5 minutes rest between each new technique set of 10 trials.
237	        The National Rugby League (NRL) Coaching Manual (31) and Tackle Safe program (14)
238	outline the technique instruction for the traditional, one-on-one, front-on, torso tackle. Detailed
239	within these manuals is instruction on how tacklers should be as upright as possible when
240	approaching the tackle, then bend their knees while keeping their shoulders higher than hip level
241	to drop their body position as they are about to execute the tackle. It outlines that tacklers should
242	use their shoulder to make the contact, and position their head to the ball carrier’s side, and
243	maintain alignment of their neck with the spine by keeping their head up and straight. To take the
244	ball carrier to the ground, the instructional manual outlines the tackler should use a strong leg drive
245	as well as use the ball carrier’s momentum. Tackle height in accordance with previous research
246	(18) is recommended in the Tackle Safe program (14) and defines torso contact as either ‘green
247	zone’ (hip area), ‘orange zone’ (mid torso, between the top of pelvis and base of chest/pectorals),
248	and ‘red zone’ (upper torso, base of chest/pectorals to line of the shoulders). In this study the tackle
249	height associated with each tackle type were: hip area (DNRL), mid torso (DTS), mid/upper torso
250	(SLP), and upper torso (SNRL), respectively (Table 1).
251	A       Table 1 details the categorisation of each of the tackle types, and how, when, and why a
252	tackler would employ each tackle type within a game is explained in detailed. The purpose of the
253	two ‘smother’ tackle types (SLP, SNRL) is to wrap up ball carriers to prevent offloading of the
254	ball, to prevent the ball carriers from using their forearm/ball as a defensive strategy to bump off
255	the tackler, and to control the ball carrier when taking the tackle to the ground in order to slow the
256	 play the ball. The two variants of the smother tackle in this study differ from one another in the
257	way the tackler engages in contact to wrap up the ball and ball carrier, and should be employed by
258	tacklers when they are on the ball carrying side of the ball carrier. In contrast, the strategy when
259	performing the two ‘dominant’ tackle instructions (DTS, DNRL) is to bring the ball carrier to the
260	ground to enable the tackler and defensive team a longer duration to get back onside for the next
261	play of the ball. The key differences between these dominant strategies are contact height and the
262	angle of the force application by the tackler (Table 1). Figure 1 outlines a tackle matrix that
263	describes when tacklers should execute a dominant tackle (i.e., when the tackler is on the non-ball
264	carrying side of the ball carrier) or a smother tackle (i.e., when the tackler is on the ball carrying
265	ide of the ball carrier) in a game situation.
266	Data Collection
267	        A full body retroreflective marker set (36) was placed on both the tackler and the ball
268	carrier participants on each of their heads, forearms, upper arms, hands, trunk, pelvis, thighs,
269	hanks, and feet. A 15 Oqus 700+ camera optoelectronic motion capture system (300 Hz; data
270	collection volume 10 m x 10 m x 6 m) using Qualisys Track Manager software (v.2018.1, Qualisys
271	AB, Göteborg, Sweden) recorded the full body three-dimensional kinematic of both participants
272	for each tackle trial. To adhere to the Nyquist sampling theorem, the sampling rate in this study
273	was determined by spectral analysis (37) of 3D head linear and angular acceleration that indicated
274	that the median frequency in which that 99% of the data occurs below was 49 Hz.
275	        Visual 3D software (Version 6, C-Motion, Germantown, MD, USA) was used to undertake
276	the three-dimensional data analysis. The raw kinematic data was interpolated with a cubic spline
277	 and then filtered by an 18 Hz cut-off frequency, zero phase fourth order low pass Butterworth
278	digital filter prior to calculating kinematic variables. An 18 Hz cut-off frequency was determined
279	by performing a residual analysis (37) of the raw 3D position of head markers with a median
280	frequency of 12 Hz (range 9 to 14 Hz) reported from the analysis. The segmental masses and
281	inertial properties were modelled as per the protocol of Schaefer et al. (2019) (36). To calculate
282	joint and segment angles a local Cartesian coordinate system was used (x-axis mediolateral; y-axis
283	anterior-posterior; and z-axis superior inferior directions).
284	        Three stages of the tackle were identified, in the following order of appearance: (i) two
285	teps prior to contact (Step 2); (ii) one step prior to contact (Step 1); and (iii) at contact, between
286	the tackler and ball carrier. These stages were defined according to the procedures outlined in
287	Edwards and colleagues (30). The tackler’s joint angles [ankle, knee, hip, lumbopelvic (lumbar
288	egment relative to the pelvis segment), thoracolumbar (lumbar segment relative to the thoracic
289	egment), trunk-pelvis (trunk segment relative to the pelvis segment)] and segment angles (thigh
290	egment, pelvis segment, and trunk segment relative to the laboratory coordinate system) at each
291	of these three sequences were reported. The resultant centre of mass velocity at the time of pre-
292	contact (defined as the maximum value prior to contact) and at contact, was used to define the
293	approach speed and speed at contact of each player.
294	Statistical Analysis
295	        Of the 600 trials collected across all 15 participants, there was a total of 455 (75.8%)
296	uccessful trials included in the statistical analysis. Unsuccessful trials were identified by the
297	expert coach during the data collection as attempts where the tackler did not adhere to the tackling
298	 instruction guidelines outlined in Table 1. Final categorization of the trials as successful or non-
299	uccessful (n = 145) was reviewed together by two authors (the expert coach and the biomechanics
300	expert) who made their decision based on viewing the Visual 3D software animation of each trial.
301	These unsuccessful trials were then excluded from the final analysis. The successful trials were
302	used to calculate the means and standard deviations for all variables across the four tackling
303	instructions when engaging in the dominant and non-dominant shoulder side for joint angles,
304	egment angles, approach speed, and speed at contact.
305	        A series of mixed general linear models were performing using IBM SPSS (Version 26.0,
306	IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Armonk, NY: IBM Corp) to determine if any significant
307	changes (p<0.05) occurred within the means of any outcome variable(s) between the four tackling
308	instruction (DNRL, DTS, SNRL and SLP). There was one repeated measure factor (step 2, step 1,
309	contact) and four subject factors of participant (n=15), instruction or tackle type (n=4), dominant
310	houlder side (n=2), and count (n=5). The ‘instruction’ factor represented the four different
311	tackling technique instructions. The ‘dominant shoulder side’ factor defined whether the tacklers
312	contacted the ball carrier’s torso with their dominant or non-dominant shoulder side. The ‘count’
313	factor defined one of the five trials performed per condition (e.g., five trials performed for DNRL
314	using the dominant shoulder side). Participant and count were included as factors to account for
315	the different number of successful trials per person within each tackle type. To determine if any
316	ignificant changes (p<0.05) occurred within peak approach speed or speed of contact between the
317	four tackle types, there were five subject factors of participant (n=15), instruction (n=4), dominant
318	houlder side (n=2), and count (n=5), player role (n=2). The ‘player role’ factor defined whether
319	the speed was of the tackler or the ball carrier.
320	         Each analysis was performed with three different repeated covariance types (compound,
321	heterogenous compound symmetry, and unstructured). As outlined by Burnham & Anderson (38),
322	the scaling criterion values were calculated using the Akaike Information Criterion from each
323	covariance type model, and the model that was selected resulted in the minimization of the scaling
324	criterion value. If the scaling criterion value was <10 between the two models, the model with the
325	less complex structure was chosen.
326	        The Akaike Information Criterion negated the requirement to satisfy the normality of
327	distribution and sphericity assumptions for each variable. Main effects of instruction, dominant
328	houlder side, and the repeated measure variable (three stages of the tackle), and their respective
329	two-way and three-way interactions were performed and pairwise contrast types were adjusted for
330	multiple comparison using least significant difference. The tackler’s rear lower limb was defined
331	as the foot that made foot-ground contact at Step 2, and lead lower limb was defined as the other
332	foot that made foot-ground contact at Step 1.
333	        The successful trials analyzed for the peak resultant head acceleration variables ranged
334	from 428 to 439 of the pool of 455 successful cases. For each angle variable across each of the
335	three time points (step 2, step 1, contact), there was a possible 1,365 cases that were inputted in
336	the mixed model general linear analysis. This led to cases included in the analyses ranging from
337	1,228 to 1,360 for joint angles and 1,296 to 1,359 for segment angles. Missing kinematic data
338	occurred in some trials because there was fewer than three retroreflective markers tracking the
339	relevant segment(s) due to marker(s) becoming occluded or unadhered to the body from body
340	contact in the tackle and/or the tackler’s sweat.
341	 RESULTS
342	Participant characteristics
343	        The participants played either both rugby codes (n = 5), only rugby league (n = 2), or only
344	rugby union (n = 8). The highest level of competition played was national (n = 1), followed by
345	tate (n = 2), regional (n = 3), and club rugby (n = 9). Playing experience was 12.7 ± 6.3 years
346	(range 4 to 30 years) with both forwards (n = 8) and backs (n = 7) included in the sample.
347	Peak Resultant Head Accelerations
348	        The DNRL (i.e., hip area) tackle type resulted in significantly higher peak resultant linear
349	and angular head accelerations for the tackler than the other three tackle types (Table 2). For the
350	ball carrier, DNRL produced the smallest peak linear and angular head accelerations. The SLP (i.e.,
351	mid/upper torso tackle type) produced lower peak resultant angular head accelerations for tacklers,
352	but higher head accelerations for ball carriers, compared to both SNRL and DTS. The ball carriers’
353	peak resultant linear head acceleration was higher during SLP compared to the SNRL and DTS.
354	Kinematics at the time of step 2, step 1, and contact
355	  C     Table 3 shows the means and standard deviations of the sagittal plane angles of various
356	joint and segment angles for the tackler during these four tackle instructions. For each tackle
357	instruction, the tackle is divided into three phases (step 2, step 1, and contact), and the dominant
358	and non-dominant side are compared for each tackle type. Supplemental Figure 2 (see
359	Supplemental Digital Content 2, http://links.lww.com/MSS/C570) provides a graphical
360	representation of the mean of all the successful trial across 15 participants for the joint and segment
361	angles from pre-tackle (0%) to post-tackle (100%) across the four tackle instructions, and a
362	 supplemental video provides animation video of these tackle instructions by a single participant
363	(see Supplemental Digital Content 3, Supplemental Video, Successful tackles exemplars,
364	http://links.lww.com/MSS/C571). The mixed general linear model of the main effects and
365	interactions of these angles are shown in Supplemental Tables 1 – 7 (upper joint angles
366	Supplemental Tables 1 – 4 and lower joint angles Supplemental Tables 5 – 7; see Supplemental
367	Digital Content 1, Results of the mixed general linear model of the main effects and interactions
368	for the tacklers, http://links.lww.com/MSS/C569). The means and standard deviations of frontal
369	and transverse joint angles (Supplemental Tables 8 – 9, see Supplemental Digital Content 1, The
370	tackler’s frontal and transverse angles, http://links.lww.com/MSS/C569) and segment angles
371	(Supplemental Tables 10 – 11, see Supplemental Digital Content 1, Table S10, The tackler’s lower
372	limb    segment       angles,
373	                              TE  and      Table     S11,     The      tackler’s     torso
374	http://links.lww.com/MSS/C569), and the results of the mixed general linear model (Supplemental
375	Tables 12 – 16, see Supplemental Digital Content 1, Results of the mixed general linear model,
376	http://links.lww.com/MSS/C569) are also in the supplemental section.
377	                                                                                               segment      angles,
378	        There were numerous differences in sagittal plane kinematics between the different types
379	of tackle instruction. Some of key findings are summarized below.
380	A       The SLP technique displayed the least head flexion at all stages of the tackle (overall, step
381	2, step 1, contact), trunk-pelvis flexion (overall, step 2, step 1, contact), thoracolumbar flexion
382	(overall, step 2, step 1, contact), lumbopelvic flexion (overall, step 2, step 1, contact), lumbopelvic
383	left lateral flexion (contact, step 2, step 1, contact), lead hip flexion (contact, step 2, step 1, contact),
384	and rear hip flexion (overall, step 1, contact) when compared to the DNRL and DTS techniques.
385	         The DNRL technique displayed the greatest head flexion (overall, step 2, step 1, contact)
386	and trunk-pelvis flexion (overall, step 1, contact) of all techniques. When compared to the DTS,
387	the DNRL also displayed greater thoracolumbar flexion (overall, step 2, step 1, contact) and lead
388	hip flexion (overall, contact, step 1).
389	Player speed
390	The ball carriers ran with a consistently higher approach speed and speed at contact than the
391	tacklers (Supplemental Table 17, see Supplemental Digital Content 1, Resultant centre of mass
392	velocity of the tackler, http://links.lww.com/MSS/C569). Peak approach speed for the tackler
393	revealed a significant main effect of tackle type and player role. The tackler’s approach speed was
394	faster in the DNRL tackle compared to all other tackle types, and the SNRL was faster than SLP
395	and DTS. The ball carrier’s approach speed was slower in a DNRL than DTS and SLP, and the
396	SNRL was slower than DTS. However, at contact, ball carriers’ speed was significantly faster when
397	being engaged in the tackle with their non-dominant shoulder side than their non-dominant
398	houlder side.
399	DISCUSSION
400	        This 3D biomechanical study examined a large dataset of successful front-on, one-on-one,
401	torso tackles. This study finds that both tackle height, and the technique used by the tackler to
402	engage in contact with the ball carrier’s torso, can alter head impact kinematics for both the tackler
403	and the ball carrier.
404	         The key outcome of this study is that the lowest torso contact height (i.e., contact at the
405	hips), which is traditionally thought to be safest and is instructed as the ‘green zone’ in coaching
406	manuals(14) (DNRL), produces the highest linear and angular head acceleration for the tackler and
407	the lowest linear and angular head acceleration for the ball carrier. Tackles that contact at the mid-
408	torso (above the hip area, but below the pectorals; DTS) or the area delineating the mid and upper
409	torso (SLP), produce lower peak head accelerations in tacklers, but higher accelerations in ball
410	carriers. Given that head injury has been found to more likely in tacklers (19), and may be the
411	result of excessive head acceleration, this finding suggests that traditional thinking about optimal
412	tackle technique, as instructed, may need to be re-evaluated, at least from the perspective of the
413	tackler, with the mid-torso the recommended target contact height. Specific findings and their
414	implications are described below.
415	Inverse relationship between peak head acceleration between the ball carrier and tackler
416	        Consistent with the literature (25), this study found that the ball carrier’s peak linear and
417	angular head acceleration increases as the contact height in the tackle increases, such that the
418	highest peak linear and angular head acceleration during front-on tackles occurs for upper torso
419	contact. Importantly, however, the opposite was found for tacklers, because the highest peak linear
420	and angular head acceleration was observed for hip area contact (DNRL), and decrease when
421	contact was mid (DTS) and mid/upper torso, particularly when the tackler was instructed in the
422	SLP method (Table 3). Considering that most head impact injuries are sustained by a tacklers rather
423	than ball carriers (10, 19, 34), tackling technique recommendations that reduce head impact
424	acceleration forces for tacklers may need to be considered as per the current study methods. This
425	recommendation must, however, be evaluated as a trade-off between tackler and ball carrier heads,
426	 because they display reciprocal peak head accelerations depending on the tackle height. Our
427	uggestion is that the modified tackle techniques described here (Table 1, see revised traffic light
428	ystem) might produce the best overall risk outcome, with the lowest head acceleraitons for
429	tacklers and moderate accelerations in ball carriers.
430	Challenging the injury safety assumptions of the NRL Tackle Safe tackle color zones based on
431	contact height
432	        The Tackle Safe program (14) recommends a ‘green zone’ (lower torso) tackle height,
433	which, from the perspective of the ball carrier, agrees with our findings and is in accordance with
434	previous research on the influence of tackle height on ball carrier head kinematics (18). It also
435	identifies an ‘orange zone’ (mid torso) and finally the ‘red zone’ (upper torso) (14). Our findings
436	challenge the safety assumptions of these color zones for the tackler. We find that the ‘green zone’
437	(i.e., DNRL) had the highest tackler peak linear and angular head acceleration when tackling front-
438	on, followed next by the ‘orange zone’ (i.e., DTS), and then the ‘orange/red zone (i.e., SLP) and
439	‘red zone’ (i.e., SNRL) with the lowest tackler head accelerations.
440	Dominant tackles have the highest head accelerations for the tacklers – recommended when
441	tacklers execute dominant tackles, they contact the ball carrier mid, not hip area
442	A       Within a team’s defensive strategy, a tackler will engage with the ball carrier’s lower torso
443	(i.e., ‘green zone’) to execute a ‘dominant tackle.’ A ‘dominant tackle’ is defined when the ball
444	carrier is moved backwards and by the completion of the tackle is taken to the ground (13). This
445	tudy suggests that the tackler’s inertial head acceleration can be decreased when performing a
446	dominant tackle by the tackler engaging at the mid (DTS i.e., ‘orange zone’), rather than the lower
447	 (DNRL, i.e., ‘green zone’) torso of the ball carrier. By executing this slightly higher torso contact
448	height at the mid torso, the tackler also adopts a more optimal ‘head up and forward’ gaze focus
449	on the ball carrier before contact (i.e., less head flexion) as well as a straight back posture (i.e., less
450	thoracolumbar flexion than in the DNRL technique). This DTS technique variant aligns better with
451	coaching recommendations (39), as well as injury risk and tackle performance evidence associated
452	with the head (39-41) and a straight back (41, 42) posture.
453	Upright tackles increase the risk of head injury – how altering the way the tackler engages in
454	contact with the ball carrier can reduce the injury risk in smother tackles
455	        Applying an intervention to lower the legal height of the tackle in professional rugby has
456	not been found to alter concussion incidence (9). The issue is that only considering one variable
457	(i.e., tackle height) may be too simplistic, and the biomechanical characteristics of the tackle and
458	the associated risk for concussion are far more complex. The present study finds that for similar
459	tackle heights (SNRL, SLP), the way the tackler was instructed to engage in contact with the ball
460	carrier when executing a smother tackle can significantly alter the head impact. The upper (SNRL)
461	and mid-upper (SLP) torso tackles performed in this study, are often known as a ‘smother tackle,’
462	because the tackler uses their chest for contact while wrapping their arms around the ball carrier
463	(43). The SLP instruction significantly reduced peak head linear acceleration compared to the
464	SNRL, DTS, and DNRL. This is important because linear head acceleration can still cause brain
465	angular acceleration without angular head acceleration when a mild deceleration of the head is
466	applied (44). When the tackler executes the SLP technique, a more optimal ‘head up and forward’
467	(i.e., less head flexion) and straight back posture (i.e., less thoracolumbar flexion, lumbopelvic
468	flexion) was attained, compared to the SNRL technique.
469	         Importantly, our mid-upper torso contacts in the SLP involved tacklers moving at relatively
470	low speeds, and under careful instruction of an expert coach in a controlled environment. The
471	point of contact between the tackler’s chest/pectoral region and the ball carrier’s body was
472	approximately the height of the sternum (i.e., intersection between mid and upper torso), not
473	higher. The tackler started from a very low position and then executed a vertical ‘pop up’ action
474	at the last moment. When engaging in contact, the tackler used his pectoral on the ball carrier’s
475	forearm and ball to wrap up both the arms around the ball carrier and then reorient the motion of
476	the ball carrier into upward direction via the ‘pop up’ action. This tackle also then moves the ball
477	carrier laterally instead of driving the ball carrier backwards to allow defensive teammates to assist
478	in the tackle. Most importantly, the tackler always positions his head outside the ball carrier
479	houlder when engaging in contact with the ball carrier.
480	        These technical cues in contact height and the way the tackler engages in contact may be
481	essential for the lower resultant head accelerations and also might reduce the tackler’s risk of
482	contact with high risk body parts (head, elbow, and shoulders) of the ball carrier. These contact
483	types, particularly head to head contacts during higher contact tackles when tacklers are upright,
484	have been found to increase the risk of head injury (10, 19, 27, 45). So there is a potential tradeoff
485	between the slightly higher torso contact we find reduces head acceleration in this study, and the
486	real world risk of such higher contact tackles leading to high risk head contacts and thus greater
487	risk as found in other studies.
488	 Player Speed
489	        Ball carriers and tacklers typically engage in a tackle at a slow speed (define as walking or
490	jogging into the tackle) (43), the tackle speed performed by both players in the current study.
491	Whether the ball carrier or tackler approaches a front-on tackle with faster speed in elite rugby
492	union remains contentious (46, 47), because nearly half of the time the ball carriers are at a higher
493	peed than the tackler (47). This study observed that the ball carriers ran significantly faster
494	approaching the tackle, and were faster at contact, despite standardizing approach distance
495	between the players in an attempt to limit the confounding effect of player speed (10, 34). This is
496	likely to reflect the time required for the tacklers to set their body position and execute the chosen
497	tackle technique, whereas in contrast the only focus of the ball carrier was to oppose the actions of
498	the tackler. These demands on the tackler are likely to have also contributed to the player’s speed
499	differing between the various techniques, when approaching the tackle, but not at contact. Both
500	NRL torso instructions (SNRL, DNRL) were performed with a faster peak approach speed by the
501	tackler than either variation of the tackling techniques (SLP, DTS), which is most likely a reflection
502	of the familiarity of the traditional tackling technique, rather than the variations in tackling
503	techniques.    C
504	  C     In contrast, in the traditional tackling types, the ball carrier approaches the tackler at a
505	lower speed than in the tackling technique variants. These speed differences may contribute partly
506	to our observed kinematic findings, particularly the reductions in head acceleration for the upper
507	torso tackles, which were variations on the typical technique and thus performed at lower tackler
508	peeds, potentially with greater caution and unfamiliarity. This may in turn have implications for
509	real-world application, because the relatively faster speeds, higher intensities, and greater
510	 unpredictability of tackles during match play may change head kinematics for any given contact
511	height and tackle technique. Further research may be required to confirm this possibility.
512	How a tackler modifies their body position to engage in different torso tackle heights is not
513	reflected by their hip and knee flexion
514	        Video analysis framework defines body position before contact as upright, medium, or low,
515	differentiated by knee and hip flexion, and body height (48). This study found that knee flexion
516	was similar across all four tackle techniques. Hip flexion did not differentiate when changing the
517	torso tackle height (i.e., SNRL versus DNRL). The 3D definition of hip flexion in this study was
518	thigh segment relative to the pelvis segment. This contrasts with the definition of hip flexion in
519	2D video analysis, where it is assessed by the thigh relative to trunk (pelvis and thorax treated as
520	ingle segment). When identifying how the tacklers executed the lower torso height in the DNRL
521	technique compared to the SNRL technique, the tacklers did not alter their knee or hip flexion,
522	however, tacklers increased their trunk-pelvis joint angle by lowering their trunk segment relative
523	to the ground. In these participants, the tacklers only decreased their tackle height by increasing
524	their trunk flexion, not their knee or hip flexion. As such, caution is warranted on how researchers
525	quantify body position prior to and at contact.
526	Understanding linear versus angular head acceleration
527	        Acceleration of the skull causes rapid deformation of brain matter that is thought to be the
528	likely cause of concussion (44). This makes intuitive sense, because the impulsive forces (incurred
529	through a rapid acceleration and deceleration) applied either directly or indirectly to the head
530	during a tackle, transfer forces through the head to the brain. Those forces can result in a
531	 concussion by placing strain on tether points within the brain that may lead to axonal stress,
532	neuroinflammation, and a neurometabolic cascade (21). This study observed that head linear
533	acceleration was significantly different between all tackling instructions, and angular acceleration
534	only differed in the DNRL. Due to anatomical constraints of these tether points on the brain, when
535	the skull decelerates the brain’s center of mass will continue to move but the tethering will cause
536	the brain to rotate (44). This is why brain angular acceleration can occur with only linear
537	acceleration of the skull when a mild deceleration of the head is applied (44), and thus both head
538	linear and angular acceleration are important to measure. Reducing the magnitude of inertial head
539	kinematics of a single tackle or across hundreds of tackles will both achieve an making tackling
540	afer regardless of either concussion injury mechanism of either an acute event (i.e., direct head
541	impact) or from sub-concussive impacts (i.e., indirect head impact). Recent attempts have been
542	made to accurately quantify and monitor a player’s in-game exposure to direct and indirect head
543	impacts in collisions sports via accelerometry (49, 50). These devices use linear acceleration
544	magnitude threshold of >5G (51) or ≥10G (49, 50, 52) to identify an impact event. These thresholds
545	are well above this current study’s average peak linear acceleration magnitude reported but are not
546	too dissimilar to a recent in-game study of professional rugby league players tackling [linear
547	(median 7.1 G, Q1 = 5.2 G, Q3 =9.9 G); and angular acceleration (median = 0.6 krad/s2, Q1 = 0.4
548	krad/s2, Q3 = 0.9 krad/s2)]. Caution is advised when comparing different methodological
549	approaches of measuring (53) and filtering (24) head impact data (i.e., head inertial kinematics)
550	and another confounding issue is the ambigious threshold of head impact data (i.e., head inertial
551	kinematics) that may cause concusssion. It is recommended that future observational or
552	interventional research investigating different tackle types measure both 3D head linear and
553	angular accleration using 3D motion capture and wearable sensors simiulataneously to clarify our
554	 understand this relationship. The unsuccessful tackles are considered as a subset of all tackles in
555	this study and should be the subject of future research to explore in detail if there is a risk that
556	when the tackler is deemed to incorrectly execute the tackle it produces undesirable inertial head
557	kinematics. This may have implications for the global head injury risk in dynamic situations where
558	tacklers do make errors, and should be a subject of future research.
559	Limitations
560	        Due to limitations to the current study, these results can only be considered as preliminary
561	and require replication in larger sample sizes. Categorization of the unsuccessful tackles by the
562	two experts as well as the expert coach potentially leading the participants when instructing the
563	techniques in this study is likely to create a risk of bias because some tackling techniques may
564	produce higher inertial head kinematics when unsuccessful. Future research should thus explore
565	tackle success in different tackle types, with a focus on outcomes when tackles are unsuccessful.
566	        Our findings may not translate to tackles involving more than one tackler, differing
567	approach direction, playing position or experience, player skill level, age, or tackles that are
568	completed by taking the ball carrier to ground. Further, the artificial laboratory environment (as
569	opposed as game environment) may have influenced the ball carrier’s and tackler’s ability to
570	perform the various tackle techniques. The study only investigated a slow tackle speed; therefore,
571	it remains unknown if altering tackling speed prior to contact changes tackling technique.
572	Furthermore, the experimental tackles were not completed to the ground, and that could further
573	reduce the generalizability of findings to actual game play. The study design does not enable any
574	further investigation of the durability of the behavioral modification (i.e., the robustness of the
575	 various tackle techniques) over longer periods of time, or the transfer of the behavioral
576	modification to match play conditions. Injury history in the subjects was not recorded, so,
577	econdary analyses could not be conducted to determine if previous injury influenced any of the
578	participants’ motion.
579	CONCLUSIONS
580	        Head inertial accelerations can be modified in a front-on, one-on-one tackle, at slow speed
581	within a single session by instructing tacklers to change the torso contact height on the ball carrier
582	and modifying the way they engage in player contact. The inclusion of a tackle specific coaching
583	instruction training program to alter the impulse forces to the head (i.e., head inertial kinematics)
584	during the tackle may be a viable concussion reduction strategy.
585	 Acknowledgements
586	The results of the present study do not constitute endorsement by American College of Sports
587	Medicine. The results of the study are presented clearly, honestly, and without fabrication,
588	falsification, or inappropriate data manipulation. Research funding support from the National
589	Rugby League (NRL) Rugby League Research Committee (RLRC) for the examination of rugby-
590	tyle tackle techniques. Mr Kim Colyvas from the Faculty of Science (The University of
591	Newcastle) Statistical Support Service for his statistical methodological guidance for this study.
592	Mr Mathew Buchanan in assisting with this study’s data collection.
593	Declaration of Conflicting Interests
594	Suzi Edwards declares that they have no conflict of interest. Andrew Gardner, Ph.D. serves as a
595	cientific advisor for hitIQ, Ltd. He has a clinical practice in neuropsychology involving
596	individuals who have sustained sport-related concussion (including current and former athletes).
597	He has been a contracted concussion consultant to Rugby Australia (2016-2020). He has received
598	travel funding or been reimbursed by professional sporting bodies, and commercial organizations
599	for discussing or presenting sport-related concussion research at meetings, scientific conferences,
